questions.prompt: Which Playwright feature gives a compact YAML view of roles and accessible names to ground AI test generation?
questions.explanation: ARIA snapshots show the real roles and names, ideal for role-based locators, and help prevent invented elements.

questions.prompt: Which locator style does the review checklist prefer?
questions.explanation: Role, label and test-id locators are resilient and readable; long CSS/XPath chains are brittle.

questions.prompt: It is fine to paste production customer data into an AI tool prompt if it helps generate realistic test data.
questions.explanation: False. Never paste secrets or production personal data into prompts; prompts may be retained depending on provider terms. Use synthetic data.

questions.prompt: What should a reviewer change in this generated test?
options: Replace the fixed wait with a web-first assertion such as expect(page.get_by_role('alert')).to_be_visible()
questions.explanation: Fixed sleeps are slow and flaky. Web-first assertions wait automatically until the condition holds.

questions.prompt: The AI suggests expected results by reading the current implementation's output. Why is that risky?
options: It encodes current behaviour, including bugs, as the oracle; expected results must come from requirements
questions.explanation: Deciding expected results has low AI helpfulness; deriving them from the implementation locks in existing bugs.

questions.prompt: What is the most direct proof that a generated test actually checks the behaviour?
options: A mutation check: deliberately break the behaviour locally and confirm the test fails
questions.explanation: A test that still passes when the behaviour is broken has a weak oracle.

questions.prompt: A self-healing tool automatically changed a locator from the 'Delete account' button to a 'Delete draft' button after a UI change, and the test is green. What is the lesson?
options: Auto-applied healing can silently test the wrong element; require human review of healing changes
questions.explanation: Auto-applying self-healing changes without human checks is a listed mistake.

questions.prompt: A team merged 300 AI-generated tests in one week, all green. Defect escape rate did not change. What most likely happened?
options: Volume was mistaken for coverage: tests were not reviewed against requirements, have weak oracles, and nobody owns them
questions.explanation: Merging green generated tests without review and lacking ownership are listed mistakes; map tests to acceptance criteria.

questions.prompt: How do you expose flakiness in newly generated tests? Select all that apply.
options: Running in random order to check independence
questions.explanation: Repeat runs and order independence expose flakiness; a single run does not.

coding.title: Review generated test code
coding.prompt:
Write `review(test_code)` returning a sorted list of issue codes found in a generated Playwright (Python) test string:

- `"fixed-wait"` if it contains `wait_for_timeout(` or `time.sleep(`
- `"xpath"` if it contains `xpath=` or a locator string starting with `//` (i.e. the text `("//` or `('//`)
- `"no-assertion"` if it contains neither `expect(` nor `assert `
- `"secret"` if it contains `password="` or `password='` followed by anything other than an `os.environ` lookup (simply: the text `password="` or `password='`)
coding.explanation: Simple static checks catch the most common weaknesses of generated tests before a human spends time on deeper review (oracle quality, reality of elements, data).

coding.title: Map tests to acceptance criteria
coding.prompt: Generated test cases arrive as a list of dicts `{"title", "requirement", "assertions": [...]}`. Write `coverage(criteria, cases)` where `criteria` is a list of requirement ids. Return `{"uncovered": [...], "no_oracle": [...], "unknown": [...]}`: criteria with no case (in criteria order), titles of cases with an empty assertion list (in order), and titles of cases referencing a requirement not in `criteria` (in order).
coding.explanation: Asking the AI for structured test cases before code lets you check intent mechanically: every criterion covered, every case with an oracle, and no invented requirements.
hints: Build the set of referenced requirements.
Use list comprehensions for each output.

tests.name: Finds all three gaps
tests.code:
cases=[{'title':'login ok','requirement':'AC1','assertions':['dashboard heading visible']},{'title':'login bad','requirement':'AC2','assertions':[]},{'title':'export pdf','requirement':'AC9','assertions':['pdf downloaded']}]
assert coverage(['AC1','AC2','AC3'],cases)=={'uncovered':['AC3'],'no_oracle':['login bad'],'unknown':['export pdf']}
